/* =============================================================
   SCOPED RESET --- nukes Shopify Dawn theme overrides
   all:initial applies to wrapper ONLY (proven pattern from live
   AP Cyber pages). Applying it to all descendants kills nested
   element display values (table cells, buttons, inline-block badges).
   ============================================================= */
#apcsa-lesson {
  all: initial !important;
  display: block !important;
  font-family: -apple-system, BlinkMacSystemFont, "Segoe UI", Roboto, "Helvetica Neue", Arial, sans-serif !important;
  max-width: 1080px !important;
  margin: 0 auto !important;
  padding: 32px 20px 80px !important;
  color: #1f2937 !important;
  -webkit-text-fill-color: #1f2937 !important;
  line-height: 1.65 !important;
  font-size: 17px !important;
  background: #ffffff !important;
}
#apcsa-lesson * {
  box-sizing: border-box !important;
}
#apcsa-lesson p, #apcsa-lesson li, #apcsa-lesson td, #apcsa-lesson th,
#apcsa-lesson dt, #apcsa-lesson dd, #apcsa-lesson span, #apcsa-lesson em, #apcsa-lesson strong {
  color: #1f2937 !important;
  -webkit-text-fill-color: #1f2937 !important;
  font-size: 17px !important;
  line-height: 1.65 !important;
}
#apcsa-lesson em { font-style: italic !important; }
#apcsa-lesson strong { font-weight: 700 !important; }
#apcsa-lesson p { margin: 0 0 16px 0 !important; }

#apcsa-lesson ol li { display: list-item !important; list-style: decimal outside !important; margin: 0 0 6px 0 !important; }

/* Headings */

  display: block !important;

  margin: 20px 0 !important;
  border-radius: 0 8px 8px 0 !important;
  border-left: 4px solid #94a3b8 !important;
  background: #f8fafc !important;
}
#apcsa-lesson .apcsa-callout h4 {
  margin-top: 0 !important;
  margin-bottom: 8px !important;
  font-size: 16px !important;

}
#apcsa-lesson .apcsa-callout.concept { background: #eff6ff !important; border-left-color: #2563eb !important; }
#apcsa-lesson .apcsa-callout.concept h4 { color: #1e3a8a !important; -webkit-text-fill-color: #1e3a8a !important; }
#apcsa-lesson .apcsa-callout.example { background: #f0fdf4 !important; border-left-color: #16a34a !important; }
#apcsa-lesson .apcsa-callout.example h4 { color: #166534 !important; -webkit-text-fill-color: #166534 !important; }
#apcsa-lesson .apcsa-callout.warning { background: #fef2f2 !important; border-left-color: #dc2626 !important; }
#apcsa-lesson .apcsa-callout.warning h4 { color: #991b1b !important; -webkit-text-fill-color: #991b1b !important; }
#apcsa-lesson .apcsa-callout.trap { background: #fef2f2 !important; border-left-color: #dc2626 !important; }
#apcsa-lesson .apcsa-callout.trap h4 { color: #991b1b !important; -webkit-text-fill-color: #991b1b !important; }

/* PRACTICE TIER */
#apcsa-lesson .apcsa-practice-tier {
  display: block !important;
  background: #fafafa !important;
  border: 1px solid #e5e7eb !important;
  border-radius: 12px !important;
  padding: 24px 28px !important;
  margin: 32px 0 !important;
}
#apcsa-lesson .apcsa-practice-tier h2 {
  margin-top: 0 !important;
  border-bottom: none !important;
  padding-bottom: 0 !important;
}
#apcsa-lesson .apcsa-practice-tier .tier-label {
  display: inline-block !important;
  background: #1e40af !important;
  color: #ffffff !important;
  -webkit-text-fill-color: #ffffff !important;
  padding: 4px 10px !important;
  border-radius: 4px !important;
  font-size: 11px !important;
  font-weight: 700 !important;
  letter-spacing: 0.08em !important;
  text-transform: uppercase !important;
  margin-right: 10px !important;
}

/* MCQ */
#apcsa-lesson .apcs-ex {
  display: block !important;
  background: #ffffff !important;
  border: 1px solid #e5e7eb !important;

  padding: 20px 22px !important;
  margin: 16px 0 !important;
}

#apcsa-lesson .apcs-ex-stem strong { color: #0f172a !important; -webkit-text-fill-color: #0f172a !important; }

#apcsa-lesson .apcs-ex-options .apcs-opt.correct { border-color: #16a34a !important; background: #dcfce7 !important; }
#apcsa-lesson .apcs-ex-options .apcs-opt.incorrect { border-color: #dc2626 !important; background: #fee2e2 !important; }
#apcsa-lesson .apcs-opt-letter {
  display: inline-block !important;
  font-weight: 700 !important;
  margin-right: 10px !important;
  color: #1e40af !important;
  -webkit-text-fill-color: #1e40af !important;
}

#apcsa-lesson .apcs-predict-gate {
  display: block !important;

  font-size: 14px !important;
  color: #78350f !important;
  -webkit-text-fill-color: #78350f !important;
  font-style: italic !important;
}

/* Buttons */
#apcsa-lesson .apcs-btn,
#apcsa-lesson .apcs-btn:link,
#apcsa-lesson .apcs-btn:visited {

  background: #2563eb !important;
  color: #ffffff !important;
  -webkit-text-fill-color: #ffffff !important;
  padding: 10px 20px !important;
  border-radius: 6px !important;
  font-weight: 600 !important;
  font-size: 15px !important;
  text-decoration: none !important;
  border: none !important;

  margin: 4px 4px 4px 0 !important;
}
#apcsa-lesson .apcs-btn:hover, #apcsa-lesson .apcs-btn:active {
  background: #1d4ed8 !important;
  color: #ffffff !important;
  -webkit-text-fill-color: #ffffff !important;
}

/* Feedback */
#apcsa-lesson .apcs-ex-feedback {

  font-size: 15px !important;
}

#apcsa-lesson .apcs-ex-feedback.fb-correct {

}
#apcsa-lesson .apcs-ex-feedback.fb-incorrect {

  -webkit-text-fill-color: #7f1d1d !important;
}

/* MASTERY */

<h2>What Is an Algorithm?</h2>
<p>An algorithm is a finite, ordered set of instructions that accomplishes a specific task. The word "finite" matters — every algorithm must eventually terminate. An infinite loop is not a valid algorithm because it never reaches a result. Algorithms are not code-specific: the same algorithm can be expressed as pseudocode, a flowchart, natural language, or Java source code. The AP exam tests your ability to recognize algorithm structure regardless of the representation used.</p>
<p>Topic 2.1 is the only topic in Unit 2 with no Java syntax requirement. The College Board assesses it using Skill 1.A — determining an appropriate program design — applied to everyday-language or diagram descriptions. Every question will ask you to identify which building blocks (sequencing, selection, repetition) are present, or to determine how order changes the outcome.</p>

<div class="apcsa-callout concept" style="margin:20px 0!important;padding:16px 20px!important;background:#ede9fe!important;border-left:4px solid #7c3aed!important;border-radius:6px!important;">

  <p style="margin:0!important;font-size:14px!important;color:#374151!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#374151!important;">"The building blocks of algorithms include sequencing, selection, and repetition." and "Algorithms can contain selection, through decision making, and repetition, via looping." Every algorithm ever written — from sorting a list to launching a rocket — is composed of only these three building blocks, combined in different orders and nestings.</p>
</div>

<h2>The Three Building Blocks</h2>
<p>Understanding these three building blocks is foundational to everything in AP CSA. Units 2 through 4 are entirely about implementing them in Java. Topic 2.1 asks you to recognize them in plain language before you write a single line of code.</p>

<div class="apcsa-callout concept" style="margin:20px 0!important;padding:16px 20px!important;background:#ede9fe!important;border-left:4px solid #7c3aed!important;border-radius:6px!important;">
  <h4 style="margin:0 0 8px!important;font-size:15px!important;color:#1e1b4b!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#1e1b4b!important;">Sequencing</h4>
  <p style="margin:0!important;font-size:14px!important;color:#374151!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#374151!important;">Statements execute one after another in the order they appear. This is the default behavior of every program. In Unit 1 you wrote nothing but sequencing: variable declarations, assignments, method calls — each running top to bottom. Sequencing alone is powerful but limited: it cannot respond to different inputs or repeat work.</p>
</div>

<div class="apcsa-callout concept" style="margin:20px 0!important;padding:16px 20px!important;background:#ede9fe!important;border-left:4px solid #7c3aed!important;border-radius:6px!important;">
  <h4 style="margin:0 0 8px!important;font-size:15px!important;color:#1e1b4b!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#1e1b4b!important;">Selection (EK 2.1.A.3)</h4>
  <p style="margin:0!important;font-size:14px!important;color:#374151!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#374151!important;">Selection occurs when execution branches based on a true/false decision. The algorithm evaluates a condition, and the result determines which path runs next. One path (or neither, in a one-way selection) executes, but never both. In Java, selection is implemented with <code>if</code>, <code>if-else</code>, and <code>if-else-if</code> statements (Topics 2.3 and 2.4).</p>
</div>

<div class="apcsa-callout concept" style="margin:20px 0!important;padding:16px 20px!important;background:#ede9fe!important;border-left:4px solid #7c3aed!important;border-radius:6px!important;">
  <h4 style="margin:0 0 8px!important;font-size:15px!important;color:#1e1b4b!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#1e1b4b!important;">Repetition (EK 2.1.A.4)</h4>
  <p style="margin:0!important;font-size:14px!important;color:#374151!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#374151!important;">Repetition is when a process repeats until a desired outcome is reached. Without repetition, processing 1,000 items would require 1,000 copies of the same code. With repetition, you write the logic once and let the loop handle the rest. In Java, repetition is implemented with <code>while</code> loops (Topic 2.7) and <code>for</code> loops (Topic 2.8).</p>
</div>

<h2>Recognizing Building Blocks in Everyday Algorithms</h2>
<p>The AP exam presents algorithms in plain English or as flowcharts and asks you to identify which building blocks are present, how many of each, or how reordering them would change the result. The key skill is translating informal descriptions into structured thinking.</p>

<div class="apcsa-callout example" style="margin:20px 0!important;padding:16px 20px!important;background:#f0fdf4!important;border-left:4px solid #16a34a!important;border-radius:6px!important;">
  <h4 style="margin:0 0 8px!important;font-size:15px!important;color:#15803d!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#15803d!important;">Worked Example — ATM Withdrawal</h4>
  <p style="margin:0 0 8px!important;font-size:14px!important;color:#374151!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#374151!important;">Read this algorithm and identify every building block:</p>
  <ol style="margin:8px 0!important;padding-left:28px!important;font-size:14px!important;color:#374151!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#374151!important;line-height:1.8!important;">
    <li>Insert card and enter PIN.</li>
    <li>If the PIN is correct, proceed. Otherwise, display "Incorrect PIN" and end.</li>
    <li>Ask the user how much to withdraw.</li>
    <li>If the requested amount exceeds the balance, display "Insufficient funds" and end.</li>
    <li>Subtract the amount from the balance.</li>
    <li>Dispense cash.</li>
    <li>Ask if the user wants another transaction. If yes, go back to step 3.</li>
  </ol>
  <p style="margin:8px 0 0!important;font-size:14px!important;color:#374151!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#374151!important;"><strong>Sequencing:</strong> steps 1, 3, 5, 6 run in order every time. <strong>Selection:</strong> steps 2 and 4 branch based on conditions (PIN correct? Amount valid?). <strong>Repetition:</strong> step 7 creates a loop back to step 3 until the user is done. All three building blocks are present.</p>
</div>

<div class="apcsa-callout example" style="margin:20px 0!important;padding:16px 20px!important;background:#f0fdf4!important;border-left:4px solid #16a34a!important;border-radius:6px!important;">
  <h4 style="margin:0 0 8px!important;font-size:15px!important;color:#15803d!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#15803d!important;">Worked Example — Mapping to Java Patterns</h4>
  <p style="margin:0 0 8px!important;font-size:14px!important;color:#374151!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#374151!important;">Even though 2.1 requires no Java, understanding what each building block becomes in code prepares you for Topics 2.3–2.8:</p>
<pre style="margin:8px 0 0!important;background:#1e293b!important;color:#e2e8f0!important;padding:14px!important;border-radius:6px!important;font-size:13px!important;overflow-x:auto!important;">// SEQUENCING: runs top to bottom, once each
int balance = 500;
int amount = 200;

// SELECTION: branches based on a condition
if (amount <= balance) {
    balance -= amount;        // path when true
} else {
    System.out.println("Insufficient funds");  // path when false
}

// REPETITION: repeats until condition is false
while (userWantsAnother) {
    amount = getUserInput();
    if (amount <= balance) {
        balance -= amount;
    }
}</pre>
</div>

<h2>Order Matters: EK 2.1.A.5</h2>
<p>The order in which sequencing, selection, and repetition are combined determines the outcome of an algorithm. This is one of the most frequently tested ideas in Topic 2.1. Two algorithms using the exact same three building blocks can produce completely different results if the order changes.</p>

<div class="apcsa-callout example" style="margin:20px 0!important;padding:16px 20px!important;background:#f0fdf4!important;border-left:4px solid #16a34a!important;border-radius:6px!important;">
  <h4 style="margin:0 0 8px!important;font-size:15px!important;color:#15803d!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#15803d!important;">Worked Example — Order Changes Everything</h4>
  <p style="margin:0 0 8px!important;font-size:14px!important;color:#374151!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#374151!important;"><strong>Algorithm A:</strong> Check if user is logged in, <em>then</em> display the dashboard, <em>then</em> load data.</p>
  <p style="margin:0 0 8px!important;font-size:14px!important;color:#374151!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#374151!important;"><strong>Algorithm B:</strong> Load data, <em>then</em> display the dashboard, <em>then</em> check if user is logged in.</p>
  <p style="margin:8px 0 0!important;font-size:14px!important;color:#374151!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#374151!important;">Algorithm A is a secure application. Algorithm B exposes private data to anyone before authentication. Same three steps, different order, completely different security behavior. On the AP exam, you may see flowchart questions asking what happens when two steps are swapped — trace the new order carefully.</p>
</div>

<div class="apcsa-callout example" style="margin:20px 0!important;padding:16px 20px!important;background:#f0fdf4!important;border-left:4px solid #16a34a!important;border-radius:6px!important;">
  <h4 style="margin:0 0 8px!important;font-size:15px!important;color:#15803d!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#15803d!important;">Worked Example — Check-Then-Loop vs. Loop-Then-Check</h4>
  <p style="margin:0 0 8px!important;font-size:14px!important;color:#374151!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#374151!important;"><strong>Check first (selection then repetition):</strong> "If there is milk, pour cereal repeatedly until bowl is full." → If there is no milk, nothing happens at all.</p>
  <p style="margin:8px 0 0!important;font-size:14px!important;color:#374151!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#374151!important;"><strong>Loop first (repetition then selection):</strong> "Pour cereal repeatedly until bowl is full, then check if there is milk." → The bowl gets filled regardless; the milk check only happens after. This produces cereal with no milk as a possible outcome.</p>
</div>

<h2>Combining Building Blocks: Real-World Scenarios</h2>
<p>Most real algorithms use all three building blocks together. The AP exam tests whether you can correctly identify which is which, and whether you can determine what happens when pieces are added, removed, or reordered.</p>

<div class="apcsa-callout example" style="margin:20px 0!important;padding:16px 20px!important;background:#f0fdf4!important;border-left:4px solid #16a34a!important;border-radius:6px!important;">
  <h4 style="margin:0 0 8px!important;font-size:15px!important;color:#15803d!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#15803d!important;">Identifying Building Blocks in Three Scenarios</h4>
  <p style="margin:0 0 4px!important;font-size:14px!important;color:#374151!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#374151!important;"><strong>Scenario 1:</strong> "Print the numbers 1 through 10."<br>
  → <strong>Repetition</strong> only (loop from 1 to 10). No decision needed.</p>
  <p style="margin:8px 0 4px!important;font-size:14px!important;color:#374151!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#374151!important;"><strong>Scenario 2:</strong> "Print only the even numbers from 1 through 10."<br>
  → <strong>Repetition</strong> (loop) + <strong>selection</strong> (check if even). Two building blocks.</p>
  <p style="margin:8px 0 0!important;font-size:14px!important;color:#374151!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#374151!important;"><strong>Scenario 3:</strong> "Set up a counter, then repeatedly ask for a number and add it to the counter until the user enters 0, then print the total."<br>
  → <strong>Sequencing</strong> (set up counter, print total) + <strong>repetition</strong> (loop until 0) + <strong>selection</strong> (check if entry is 0). All three building blocks.</p>
</div>

<div class="apcsa-callout trap" style="margin:20px 0!important;padding:16px 20px!important;background:#fef3c7!important;border-left:4px solid #d97706!important;border-radius:6px!important;">

  <p style="margin:0!important;font-size:14px!important;color:#374151!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#374151!important;">"The vending machine checks each of the 8 item slots to see if they are sold out." This uses <strong>repetition</strong> (check 8 times) and <strong>selection</strong> (sold out?). Students often say "selection only" because they focus on the decision. Count how many times the decision happens: if it happens repeatedly, repetition is also present.</p>
</div>

<div class="apcsa-callout trap" style="margin:20px 0!important;padding:16px 20px!important;background:#fef3c7!important;border-left:4px solid #d97706!important;border-radius:6px!important;">
  <h4 style="margin:0 0 8px!important;font-size:15px!important;color:#92400e!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#92400e!important;">AP Trap: "Sequencing Only" Is Rarer Than You Think</h4>
  <p style="margin:0!important;font-size:14px!important;color:#374151!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#374151!important;">Pure sequencing means no decisions and no repetition at all. Most real algorithms have at least one condition. If you are tempted to answer "sequencing only," verify there truly is no branch and no loop anywhere in the description before committing to that answer.</p>
</div>

<div class="apcsa-callout trap" style="margin:20px 0!important;padding:16px 20px!important;background:#fef3c7!important;border-left:4px solid #d97706!important;border-radius:6px!important;">

  <p style="margin:0!important;font-size:14px!important;color:#374151!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#374151!important;">If an AP exam question shows a flowchart and asks "what happens if step X and step Y are swapped," you must trace the new order from scratch. Do not assume the result is the same. This EK is directly tested: the order in which sequencing, selection, and repetition are used contributes to the outcome.</p>
</div>

<h2>Real-World Connection</h2>
<p>Every piece of software ever written is built from these three blocks. A GPS routes you using repetition (check location every second) and selection (if you have left the route, recalculate). A hospital monitoring system uses repetition (check vitals every 30 seconds) and selection (if heart rate exceeds threshold, alert staff). A spreadsheet formula uses sequencing (evaluate each cell in order) and selection (IF functions). Recognizing these patterns in descriptions of systems you already use every day is exactly the skill Topic 2.1 develops — and it transfers directly to reading and writing Java code in every remaining unit of this course.</p>

<h2>Summary</h2>
<ul style="font-size:14px!important;line-height:1.8!important;color:#374151!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#374151!important;">
  <li>
<strong>Three building blocks:</strong> sequencing, selection, and repetition. Every algorithm uses some combination of these.</li>
  <li>
<strong>Sequencing</strong> = run in order, once each. Default program flow.</li>
  <li>
<strong>Selection</strong> = branch based on a true/false condition. One path (or neither) runs.</li>
  <li>
<strong>Repetition</strong> = loop until a desired outcome. The block runs zero or more times.</li>
  <li>
<strong>Order matters (EK 2.1.A.5):</strong> swapping the position of building blocks can completely change algorithm behavior.</li>
  <li>
<strong>Topic 2.1 is conceptual:</strong> recognize these patterns in plain language and flowcharts. No Java syntax required by the CED for this specific topic.</li>
  <li>
<strong>Flowcharts:</strong> diamonds = selection, rectangles = sequencing/action, back-arrows = repetition.</li>
</ul>
<h2>The Three Building Blocks of Algorithms</h2>
<p>Every algorithm — no matter how complex — is built from just three components. You already know one from Unit 1.</p>

<div class="apcsa-callout concept">
  <h4>Sequencing</h4>
  <p>Statements execute in order, one after another. This is what you practiced throughout Unit 1: declarations, expressions, method calls — each running in sequence.</p>
</div>

<div class="apcsa-callout concept">
  <h4>Selection</h4>
  <p><strong>Selection</strong> occurs when a choice of how execution will proceed is based on a true or false decision. The algorithm branches: one path executes if the condition is true, a different path (or nothing) if it’s false.</p>
</div>

<div class="apcsa-callout concept">
  <h4>Repetition</h4>
  <p><strong>Repetition</strong> is when a process repeats itself until a desired outcome is reached. Instead of writing the same code ten times, you write it once inside a loop.</p>
</div>

<h2>Selection in Everyday Life</h2>
<p>Selection is everywhere. Your phone’s autocorrect uses selection: <em>if the word is misspelled, suggest a correction.</em> A streaming app uses selection: <em>if the user is a subscriber, show the full catalog.</em></p>

<div class="apcsa-callout example">
  <h4>Selection: Real-World Pattern</h4>
  <p>A vending machine checking if a customer paid enough:</p>
  <pre>if (amountInserted >= itemPrice) {
    dispenseItem();
} else {
    returnMoney();
}</pre>
  <p>The machine makes a decision based on a true/false condition.</p>
</div>

<h2>Repetition in Everyday Life</h2>
<p>Repetition handles tasks that need to happen multiple times. A car wash repeats its scrubbing cycle for every car. An email app checks for new mail repeatedly on a timer.</p>

<div class="apcsa-callout example">
  <h4>Repetition: Real-World Pattern</h4>
  <p>A cashier scanning items one by one until there are no more:</p>
  <pre>while (moreItems) {
    scanNextItem();
    updateTotal();
}</pre>
  <p>The process repeats until the desired outcome (all items scanned) is reached.</p>
</div>

<h2>Order Matters</h2>
<p>The order in which sequencing, selection, and repetition appear changes the result of an algorithm. Consider two versions of checking a PIN:</p>

<div class="apcsa-callout warning">
  <h4>AP Trap: Order Changes the Outcome</h4>
  <p>Checking the PIN <em>before</em> allowing access vs. <em>after</em> produces entirely different behavior. Always trace through the exact order of execution when analyzing algorithms.</p>
</div>
